Duke Austin, asked where else he would add manufacturing after transformers and a utility pole company: 'We did the breaker deal with HICO. I thought that was a critical path for us and the high-voltage breakers are very difficult to get. You've seen us build them and partner.' He will stay selective - EBOS companies are explicitly not a focus. The other leg is integrated fabrication: about seven million square feet of fabrication space, plus roughly 0.5 million square feet added with the recent acquisitions, with VDC (virtual design and construction) engineering in front of it so modules are designed for constructability. Quanta sells direct to the hyperscalers and to the larger technology customers, and can self-perform 'call it 80% of what a data center build is, maybe 90%', taking balance-of-plant scope and full-scale data-center opportunities on more and more sites; it is also picking up work at semiconductor plants, at manufacturing and medical facilities, and at Tesla. The pitch is speed and certainty: 'Technology is trying to move as fast as possible. Utilities are working to protect the ratepayer, and Quanta sits in the middle of that nexus.' On state-level data-center moratoriums (New York): immaterial - 'nothing really gets built there' - and these are eight- to ten-year developments, not one-year builds, with multiyear projects extending well beyond 2030.

quarterly_data.signal: WHERE THE BOTTLENECK ACTUALLY IS: interconnection and utility-scale generation, not Quanta's labour. Duke Austin: 'I'm not sure people understand that nexus and how difficult it is to interconnect to the grid and how much we're right in the middle of that interconnection', pointing at 'the queues on the utility side of substations, all the substations that are out there. We're right in the middle of that.' 'It takes generation and substations to get to the queue', and many data centers want to connect back to the grid at some point, which utilities do better than anyone. On generation he says it is 'technically difficult to have capacity to build combined cycles at the levels and speed desired', and that orders for engines placed today often carry a five- to six-year lead time - which he reads as evidence of how long this build lasts. Quanta does EPC on generation both in front of the meter and behind the meter, small engines through big engines, but will not take the risk on the combined-cycle side and some single-cycle engines without the contract terms it needs; some utilities are attempting to self-perform gas generation RFPs because of inadequate resources, which he has seen fail before.

quarterly_data.signal: REGULATORY UNLOCK FOR LARGE LOADS moving far faster than expected. FERC in June ordered EVERY RTO to justify (or revise) how its tariff provides just and reasonable interconnection of LARGE LOADS, and directed PJM to explain why co-located transmission services cannot be made available more quickly; FERC is also willing to study GENERATION AND LOAD TOGETHER AT A COMMON POINT OF INTERCONNECTION, which Constellation has advocated. PJM released proposals for the RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT (RBP) and INTERIM RESOURCE ADEQUACY SERVICE (IRAS), set a target of 6.8 GW for the RBP, and is running a BILATERAL MATCHMAKING process to pair customers with new supply and shrink the centrally procured amount; the RBP auction is proposed for this fall with RESULTS BY YEAR-END. Co-location rule clarity is now expected in Q1-Q2 2027 (PJM response due ~November 2026, FERC order Q1-Q2 2027) versus PJM's earlier 2029 target. Separately Constellation is urging the EPA to exclude FERC-tariff-directed curtailments from the 50-HOUR ANNUAL LIMIT on data-center BACKUP GENERATORS, which management says may be the most effective way to cover the few peak hours
quarterly_data.figure: PJM RBP target 6.8 GW, auction this fall; co-location clarity Q1-Q2 2027 (was 2029)

quarterly_data.signal: THE STRANDED-CAPACITY THESIS, restated as the core commercial argument: the grid has unused generation and wires capacity in OVER 99% OF THE HOURS of the year - 'we have a peak capacity concern, not an energy concern' - so the fastest and cheapest path to powering AI is harvesting that latent capacity and managing the handful of peak hours with batteries, demand response, peaking resources and customer backup generation. Management argues existing and new supply are not bifurcated: even a customer that self-manages peaks via Connect and Manage 'will still need to buy energy for all of the other hours', which is where the existing fixed-price, carbon-free nuclear fleet becomes the multi-decade product customers want. Customer sophistication about the grid is now 'as good as the energy companies themselves' - not true two years ago. Management expects the data economy to invest 'upwards of $1 trillion in infrastructure ANNUALLY' and expects PJM deal flow to 'kick off with a bit of a bang' once rules are final
quarterly_data.figure: grid unused >99% of hours; data economy capex 'upwards of $1T annually'

Combined, those four projects represent 6 GW of newly contracted customer load, and together with agreements previously signed they bring total contracted large load agreements across Southern's electric subsidiaries to over 17 GW by the mid-2030s. CEO Christopher Womack framed the vertically integrated, state-regulated model (one-stop shop across generation, transmission and distribution) as the differentiator winning hyperscaler and data-center developer business in the Southeast.

Beyond the 17 GW already contracted there are an additional 8 GW of projects in late stages, including 3 GW projected to be finalized in the near term; CFO David Poroch said those contracts are likely to go into 2028 and beyond, with a couple of them initiating their ramp-up in 2028 and running into the next decade. System-wide data-center load now exceeds 1.2 GW, an increase of more than 500 megawatts over the prior year, and Poroch noted the company 'crossed over the 1,000 MW line this particular quarter.' Data-center usage was 55% higher than Q2 2025 and is up 49% year to date, primarily due to accelerating load ramps from large-load customers. That pulled weather-normal commercial sales up 7.4% in Q2 (+6% year to date) and total weather-normal retail electricity sales up 2.3% in the first half - the highest retail sales growth through June in nearly two decades. quarterly_data.signal: HOW THE AI-LOAD CONTRACTS ARE CREDIT-PROTECTED - ABOUT $21 BILLION OF COLLATERAL BEHIND 17 GW. The large-load contracting framework has four pillars: long-term contracts (the OpenAI contract is 25 years), minimum bills covering at least 100% of the incremental cost to serve, default/termination provisions, and default payments tied to collateral. Poroch said forms of collateral include parent guarantees, lines of credit and surety bonds depending on counterparty credit quality, with the aim of a collateral portfolio equivalent to about A- or better. He initially cited '$20.8 billion of collateral... in the aggregate on full ramp' and then clarified that this refers to the entire portfolio: 'the whole portfolio of the 17 GW, we got about $21 billion of collateral.' Minimum bills effectively decouple revenue from actual customer ramp rates, which Womack said often differ from what was predicted at project approval.

CFO Jeanne Jones attributes the cut not to demand weakness but to Exelon's own screening discipline: it developed TRANSMISSION SECURITY AGREEMENTS (TSAs) that 'never existed in our regions', and its cluster process now requires a customer to sign a TSA and, importantly, 'PUT UP COLLATERAL BEHIND THAT'. The result: 'what this update reflects is we have now WEEDED OUT SPECULATIVE PROJECTS, and it gives us proactive insight into what is real.' Exelon says it has deliberately kept capex increases consistent with historical levels and only committed capital that was 'certain and durable', alongside its stance on CO-LOCATION and fair cost allocation to shield existing customers from infrastructure costs. This is a useful reality-check datapoint on how much of the headline AI interconnection queue is firm versus speculative.

quarterly_data.signal: Component shortages were the quarter's defining constraint. Critical suppliers 'essentially shut a lot of us down with a hard stop' and the shortages hit faster and lasted longer than anticipated; Modine had previously flagged four suppliers as potential vulnerabilities in its risk-management process. Because plants were already being staffed and prepared for significantly higher volume, the part shortages caused temporary downtime and lower-than-planned capacity utilisation across the expansion sites: excess labour plus unfavourable overhead absorption on the lower volumes had a 450-550 basis point impact on Data Center margin in the quarter, on top of a 150 basis point year-over-year warranty variance from a large prior-year settlement. Modine repositioned available parts to its highest-producing, most efficient lines and idled others, and rationed supply so that its largest key accounts got priority over smaller customers. By the third month of the quarter (June) Data Center margin was 'right back where we'd expect it to be,' and management said it has now secured the supply chain needed to meet demand for the rest of the year.

Data center margins are accretive to overall Commercial HVAC margins (CSA Commercial in the mid to high teens).

quarterly_data.signal: Driven by data centers, the Middle East delivered sales growth of about 35% in the quarter despite a very challenging operating environment; in China, Commercial HVAC saw nice data center orders in July alongside electronics fab demand.
quarterly_data.figure: Middle East sales +35% driven by data centers

quarterly_data.signal: Carrier's second-quarter 2026 earnings release shows Climate Solutions Americas (CSA) segment net sales of $3,372 million versus $3,252 million a year earlier (+4%), with organic sales up 4% driven by Residential and Light Commercial (up 9% and 10%), partially offset by Commercial (excluding NORESCO) down 8% due to the timing of customer deliveries; segment operating margin was 24.4% versus 27.0%. Scope: CSA is Carrier's Americas segment combining Residential, Light Commercial and Commercial HVAC, so the segment total is not a data-center-only figure; the release does not break out data-center sales within it.
quarterly_data.figure: CSA net sales $3,372 million vs $3,252 million (+4%), three months ended June 30, 2026; CSA Commercial down 8%; segment operating margin 24.4% vs 27.0%
